title: Bean lifecycle and @PostConstruct
summary: Initialization order, Jakarta imports, startup hooks, and shutdown boundaries.

sources.title: Engineering Digest: Mastering @PostConstruct in Spring Boot: Complete Guide for Developers
Spring Framework: initialization and destruction callbacks
Spring Boot: application events and listeners

richText: A bean is an object managed by the Spring container. For a normal singleton bean, Spring constructs it, supplies its dependencies, then runs initialization callbacks.
@PostConstruct marks an initialization method called after dependency injection. Use it when initialization needs another bean or an injected property.
For Spring Boot 3, import jakarta.annotation.PostConstruct. Older Spring Boot 2 code commonly uses javax.annotation.PostConstruct.
A constructor should establish the object’s required state. A field injected after construction is unavailable inside that constructor.
A singleton initialization callback runs for that bean instance when it is initialized. It does not run for every request.
Constructor injection allows the initialization method to use a dependency whose presence is guaranteed.
SettingsRepository in the example is an application-defined collaborator. Its loadRequiredSettings method must fail clearly if required settings cannot be loaded.
Use @PostConstruct for local bean initialization. Use ApplicationRunner or CommandLineRunner for work intended to run after SpringApplication has initialized the context.
Use ApplicationReadyEvent when work must wait until startup runners have completed. It is an application startup signal, not a recurring timer.
Avoid long remote calls in bean initialization unless startup must depend on their result. Timeouts and a clear failure policy prevent an indefinite startup wait.
@PostConstruct is not a transaction boundary. A callback on the bean itself may run before its transactional proxy is available.
Use @PreDestroy for managed shutdown cleanup. Process termination can still prevent callbacks from completing; cleanup is not a delivery guarantee.
A cache loaded at startup needs a refresh policy if its source can change. A one-time callback alone does not keep cached settings current.
